opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it is quite human, and I don't say that to blame anyone. When you're working on something every day, when your identity, your career, your colleagues, and in some cases a lot of money are tied up in it, it's very hard psychologically to entertain the idea that what you're doing could be deeply harmful. We all want to feel that we're the good guys. So there's a natural pull toward stories that let you keep doing what you're doing and feel good about it.

I recognize this in myself, actually. For many years I was aware of the arguments about catastrophic risks from AI, and I sort of brushed them aside. It wasn't because I had carefully refuted them. It was more that it was uncomfortable to think my life's work could contribute to something terrible. It took ChatGPT and the realization that things were moving much faster than I had expected, and also thinking about my children and grandchild, to really confront it emotionally and not just intellectually.

There's also a selection effect. People who are very worried about the risks are less likely to join a company racing to build ever more capable systems, or they leave. So the people who remain tend, on average, to be more optimistic. Then you have the group dynamics: if everyone around you thinks things will be fine, it becomes the default view, and voicing serious concern can feel like disloyalty or a career risk.

And then there's the competitive framing, which I think is very powerful. "If we don't do it, someone less careful will." There's some truth in that, but it can also become a rationalization for accelerating in a way that nobody, collectively, would choose if we could coordinate.

To be clear, I'm not saying optimism is always wrong. There are genuinely good reasons to think the benefits could be enormous. But when we're talking about risks that could be irreversible, even catastrophic for humanity, the right attitude isn't optimism or pessimism. It's humility. We don't know how to make sure these systems will behave as intended once they're smarter than us. When you don't know, and the stakes are that high, the precautionary principle should apply. And I worry that the incentives in these companies push people away from that kind of humility.

r001.rationale: The candidate says employees are drawn to stories that let them continue their work and feel good about it, because their identities and careers are tied to the work.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think I understand it from the inside, in a sense, because I was in that position for most of my career. For decades I was building these systems, and I was excited about the science and about the potential benefits — in medicine, in climate, in education. When you are in that mindset, you are focused on what the technology can do for people, and the risks feel abstract and far away. So I don't think most of these people are lying or cynical. I think there is a very human tendency to believe things that are convenient for us, especially when our identity, our status, and our income are tied to the thing in question.

There is also something psychological about it. If you work every day on building something, and you believe it could be extremely dangerous, that creates a kind of internal conflict that is hard to live with. So the mind finds ways to resolve it. You tell yourself, "Well, it's better that I'm doing it than someone less careful," or "We'll solve the safety problems when we get there," or "The dangers are overblown." And these are not crazy arguments — some of them may even be partly true. But I notice that the conclusions people reach correlate very strongly with where their interests lie, and that should make all of us suspicious, including about our own reasoning.

What changed for me, around early 2023, was realizing that the timelines might be much shorter than I had assumed. For a long time I thought human-level AI was decades away, maybe centuries, so it was a philosophical question. When I started to feel that it could happen in five, ten, twenty years, then it became a question about my children and my grandchildren, and I could no longer put it aside. And when I looked honestly at what we actually know about controlling these systems, the answer is that we don't know how to do it. We don't have the scientific understanding to guarantee that a system more capable than us will behave the way we want. That's not a reason for panic, but it is a reason for humility.

So when I hear people at the companies say, "Don't worry, it will be fine," my question is: on what basis? Is it based on evidence, on a theory, on experiments? Or is it based on the fact that it would be very inconvenient if it weren't fine? And I think, most often, it's the latter. There is also a commercial race, and the race itself distorts judgement. Even people who are privately worried feel they cannot slow down, because the competitor won't. So optimism becomes almost a necessary posture to keep going. And I would add that it's not only the companies — many of my academic colleagues share this optimism, often for a different reason, which is a kind of pride that we would be able to anticipate and handle whatever comes.

I prefer to think about it in terms of uncertainty and stakes. Maybe they are right and I am wrong. I would be very happy to be wrong. But if there is even a modest probability of catastrophic outcomes — and I think there is, and I think many of them would admit that privately — then the rational response is not to be optimistic or pessimistic, it is to be careful. We buy insurance for our houses even if we think they probably won't burn down. The stakes here are much higher than a house. So I would ask the optimists not to abandon their hopes, but to act as if they might be wrong, and to support the kinds of safeguards, regulation, and scientific work that would protect us in that case.

r001.rationale: The candidate says employees’ identity, status, and income are tied to their work, making it psychologically convenient to believe the technology will turn out well; it also says their conclusions track their interests.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of that optimism is sincere. People working on AI see the potential benefits very clearly, and those benefits could be enormous—in science, in medicine, in helping people. That’s part of what motivated me to work on AI for so many years.

But we also have to recognise that our beliefs are influenced by our interests and by the people around us. If your work is exciting, if it brings you recognition and financial rewards, and if your colleagues all believe that you’re building something wonderful, it becomes harder to take seriously the possibility that you’re also creating something dangerous. That doesn’t require anybody to be dishonest. It’s a very human phenomenon.

I would distinguish optimism about what AI could do from confidence that it will turn out well. We can have ambitious hopes for the benefits while acknowledging that we don’t yet know how to control systems much more capable than ourselves. The hopes don’t resolve that uncertainty. We need evidence and safeguards, rather than relying on the good intentions of the people building these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says that exciting work, recognition, financial rewards, and colleagues’ enthusiasm can make AI employees less willing to take dangerous outcomes seriously, describing a bias toward beliefs that affirm their work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think much of that optimism is sincere. People working on AI see the potential benefits very clearly, and there are good reasons to be excited. AI could help us make scientific discoveries, develop medicines, and improve people’s lives.

But we also have to recognize that our judgments are influenced by our motivations. If your work, your professional identity, and perhaps your financial interests depend on this technology succeeding, it becomes harder to take seriously the possibility that it could have catastrophic consequences. That doesn’t mean you’re dishonest. It’s a very human kind of bias, and scientists aren’t immune to it.

So I would distinguish being optimistic about what AI could do from being confident that things will go well. We can pursue the benefits while acknowledging that there are serious uncertainties and that we need safeguards. Hoping for a good outcome is not, by itself, a reason to believe we’ll get one.

r001.rationale: The response says employees’ work and professional identity can make it harder to take seriously catastrophic outcomes, describing this as a human bias. This clearly links their optimism to expectations that feel good about their own work.
